idiom_name: internal declarations at the module boundary with a public interface
implementation_notes: Kotlin's internal modifier is the language-level firewall: a declaration is visible everywhere inside the same module (a Gradle source set, Maven project or IDE module) and invisible to consumers, so an internal class implementing a public interface plus a factory or DI binding replaces the wrapper class, and the published API is exactly the public declarations. The ABI half is the platform's job - Kotlin compiles to JVM class files, so private members never force dependents to recompile - and apiDump plus the binary-compatibility validator keep the published surface honest. Note that internal is a compile-time notion erased to public with a mangled name in bytecode, so Java code in the same module can still see it.
pitfalls: internal is module-wide, not package-wide, and a module is whatever the build compiles together: splitting a library into more artifacts or merging source sets silently changes who can see the implementation, with no compiler warning.

In bytecode internal members are public with mangled names, so Java code in the same module and reflection can still reach them; never treat internal as a security boundary or as a way to hide secrets.

Inline functions that read internal or private members make the compiler emit accessors that become part of the binary API (SIP-52 added @publicInBinary for this), so avoid inline over implementation details in published libraries.
